extracted.intended_audience: employers/agents petitioning for H-1B workers and prospective H-1B beneficiaries
extracted.subtask_description: Official USCIS guidance on eligibility, documentation, filing steps, and regulatory requirements for H-1B specialty occupation classifications, including subcategories (H-1B2, H-1B3), LCA rules, cap/registration rules, portability, and related payment/exception rules. Useful for employers, immigration attorneys, and applicants preparing or reviewing H-1B petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialty occupation core definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The occupation requires: (1) theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized knowledge; and (2) attainment of a bachelor's or higher degree in a directly related specific specialty (or its equivalent) as a minimum for entry into the occupation in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational eligibility test for H-1B classification; the position must satisfy both the specialized-knowledge and degree-requirement elements. See 8 CFR references provided on the page for further legal detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position-level specialty occupation criteria (one-of-four)
rubrics_metrics.description: The position must meet one of the following to qualify as a specialty occupation: (1) A U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree in a directly related specific specialty, or equivalent, is normally the minimum entry requirement for the occupation; (2) such a degree is normally required to perform job duties in parallel positions among similar organizations in the employer’s industry in the U.S.; (3) the employer (or third party) normally requires such a degree to perform the job duties; or (4) the specific duties are so specialized, complex, or unique that the knowledge required is normally associated with attainment of such a degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of these criteria, 'normally' means usual/typical/common, not always. 'Directly related' means a logical connection between the required degree and the duties. See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(A) and (ii) for regulatory language and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficiary qualification options (one-of-four)
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify to perform services in a specialty occupation the beneficiary must meet one of: (1) hold a U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree required by the specialty occupation from an accredited institution; (2) hold a foreign degree equivalent to a U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree required by the specialty occupation; (3) hold an unrestricted state license/registration/certification authorizing full practice in the specialty in the state of intended employment; or (4) have education, specialized training, and/or progressively responsible experience equivalent to a U.S. bachelor’s or higher degree and recognition of expertise through progressively responsible positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degrees must be directly related to the specialty. The equivalent-experience route requires clear documentation of how training/experience maps to the degree equivalency. See cited 8 CFR provisions for additional detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor Condition Application (LCA) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Form ETA-9035/9035E certified by the Department of Labor must be included with Form I-129 for specialty occupation and fashion model petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The LCA includes attestations and evidence; the petition will not be properly filed without a certified LCA when required. See the DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification for certification procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: LCA attestations and employer obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: By filing the LCA, the employer/agent attests that it will: (1) pay the H-1B worker a wage no less than similarly qualified workers or the prevailing wage (whichever is greater); (2) provide working conditions that will not adversely affect similarly employed workers; (3) there is no strike or lockout at the place of employment at the time of the LCA; and (4) notice of filing has been given to the bargaining representative or posted at the workplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of LCA attestations can result in fines, bars on sponsoring nonimmigrant or immigrant petitions, and other sanctions. Employers must maintain and be able to present supporting documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: H-1B licensing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the occupation in the state of intended employment requires a state or local license to fully practice the specialty occupation, the beneficiary generally must have that license before the petition is approved (not just at time of filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a required license is not evidenced at filing, USCIS will generally issue a request for evidence (RFE). See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(4)(v)(A)–(B) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic registration and cap-subject filing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For cap-subject H-1B petitions, USCIS will not consider a petition properly filed unless it is based on a valid, selected electronic registration for the same beneficiary and fiscal year (unless registration is suspended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS implemented electronic registration in 2020; employers must submit registrations during the registration period (typically March). Selected registrants are notified and may file petitions during the applicable filing period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition filing process and required documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise filing: (1) Employer/Agent obtains DOL-certified LCA (only required for specialty occupation and fashion model petitions); (2) Employer/Agent files completed Form I-129 at the correct location or online and includes the certified LCA and any required evidence (including, when subject to the Presidential Proclamation, proof of the $100,000 payment scheduled or evidence of an exception); (3) If approved and the worker is outside the U.S., the worker applies for an H-1B visa or admission with DOS/CBP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the I-129 Direct Filing Chart and Form I-129 instructions. Failure to include required LCA or payment proof (when applicable) will result in denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Proclamation $100,000 payment — applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain H-1B petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 21, 2025, filed on behalf of beneficiaries who are outside the U.S. and do not have a valid H-1B visa (or that request consular notification/port of entry/pre-flight inspection) must be accompanied by an additional $100,000 payment as a condition of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proclamation also applies in some change-of-status/amendment/extension filings if USCIS determines the alien is ineligible for change of status (e.g., not in valid status or departs before adjudication). The Proclamation does not apply to previously issued valid H-1B visas or petitions submitted prior to the effective date. See the 'Who is subject' section and exceptions below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Proclamation $100,000 payment — how and when to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners must submit the required $100,000 payment using pay.gov (H-1B Visa Payment to Remove Restriction). Payment must be made before filing the petition, and petitioners must submit proof that the payment has been scheduled from pay.gov or evidence of an exception at time of filing. Petitions filed without payment proof or exception evidence will be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow pay.gov instructions and include the proof with Form I-129 filing. USCIS will deny petitions missing this requirement when it applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Proclamation exceptions process
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to the $100,000 payment are granted by the Secretary of Homeland Security only in extraordinarily rare circumstances where the Secretary determines the worker’s presence is in the national interest, no American worker is available, the worker does not pose a threat to security/welfare, and requiring the payment would significantly undermine U.S. interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers who believe a worker meets this high threshold may seek an exception by sending a request and supporting evidence to H1BExceptions@hq.dhs.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: H-1B2 (DOD researcher) eligibility and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: For H-1B2 classification (DOD researcher and development project worker) the job must require a bachelor’s or higher degree (or equivalent) and the petition must be accompanied by: a verification letter from the DOD project manager stating the beneficiary will work on a cooperative R&D or coproduction project under a reciprocal government-to-government agreement; a general description of duties and actual employment dates on the project; and a statement listing aliens currently employed on the project (with dates) and those whose employment ended within the past year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific project details are not required in the DOD verification letter. Beneficiary education/experience requirements mirror the general H-1B qualification options (degree, equivalent, license, or equivalent experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: H-1B3 (fashion model) eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The position or services must require a fashion model of prominence, and the beneficiary must be a fashion model of distinguished merit and ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An LCA is required with Form I-129 for fashion model petitions. Evidence should demonstrate prominence and distinguished merit/ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of stay and standard validity limits
rubrics_metrics.description: H-1B workers may generally be admitted for up to 3 years initially, with the initial period extendable for an additional up to 3 years for a total of 6 years. If the beneficiary has controlling interest (>50% ownership or majority voting rights) in the petitioning organization, the initial petition and first extension approvals are each limited to up to 18 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard extensions beyond six years are limited and subject to the special provisions described separately (approved immigrant petition / labor certification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension beyond sixth year — approved immigrant petition basis
rubrics_metrics.description: You may be eligible for an H-1B extension beyond the sixth year if you are the beneficiary of an approved immigrant visa petition under EB-1, EB-2, or EB-3 and are otherwise eligible but for visa availability; petitioners must demonstrate the immigrant visa is not available as of the date they file an H-1B petition with USCIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS may grant extensions in up to 3-year increments until a final decision on the immigrant petition or adjustment of status is made, or the immigrant petition approval is revoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension beyond sixth year — 365-day labor certification/filing basis
rubrics_metrics.description: You may be eligible for an H-1B extension beyond the sixth year if at least 365 days have passed since a permanent labor certification was filed with DOL on your behalf (if required) or an immigrant visa petition was filed with USCIS on your behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions under this provision may be granted in up to 1-year increments until the permanent labor certification expires or an immigration decision is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusing failure to timely file adjustment/application within 1-year
rubrics_metrics.description: You are ineligible for certain extensions if you fail to file an adjustment of status application or apply for an immigrant visa within 1 year of an immigrant visa being available, but USCIS may excuse such failure if the employer establishes the failure was due to circumstances beyond the beneficiary’s control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will consider the totality of circumstances, including whether there was a change of employment, whether the change was voluntary, when/why employment with the original employer ended, and steps taken by the beneficiary and new employer to file. Both voluntary and involuntary employment changes may be excused where circumstances justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer liability for return transportation on termination
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer terminates the H-1B worker’s employment before the end of the authorized period of stay, the employer will be liable for the reasonable costs of return transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the beneficiary voluntarily resigns, the employer is not responsible for return transportation costs. See USCIS options guidance for workers following termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: H-1B cap numerical limits and exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual numerical limit (cap) of 65,000 new statuses/visas each fiscal year plus an additional 20,000 for beneficiaries with a U.S. master’s degree or higher. H-1B workers petitioned by institutions of higher education or affiliated/related nonprofit entities, nonprofit research organizations, or government research organizations are cap-exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the H-1B Cap Season page for details on cap mechanics and exemptions (including H-1B1 set-asides and usage adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability — changing employers (when work may begin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If changing H-1B employers, the beneficiary may begin working for the new employer as soon as the new employer properly files a non-frivolous Form I-129 petition on the beneficiary’s behalf, or as of the requested start date on that petition, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be eligible for portability, you must not have been employed without authorization since your last admission to the U.S., and the new employer must file the new petition before your H-1B authorized stay expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability — work authorization during adjudication and denial consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligible for portability, employment with the new employer is authorized until USCIS decides on the I-129. If the new petition is approved, work continues for the approved period. If denied, authorization to work based on portability ceases on denial; the beneficiary may continue working for the previous employer if the prior authorization period is still valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beneficiaries should monitor petition status and maintain lawful status; layoff rules (see grace period) may affect options upon denial or termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period after employment ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are laid off, fired, quit, or otherwise cease employment, you may have up to 60 consecutive days or until the end of your authorized validity period (whichever is shorter) to find new employment, change status, or depart the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 60-day period is the standard portability/severance grace period USCIS describes for H-1B workers; eligibility to use it depends on your specific circumstances and prior authorized stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cap-subject petition timing and requested start date constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: H-1B cap petitions must have a start date of Oct. 1 (or later) of the applicable fiscal year and may not be filed more than 6 months before the requested start date on the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic registration selection is separate and governs who may file; only those with a valid selected registration should file cap-subject petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent employment — cap-exempt to cap-subject interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: If currently employed in a cap-exempt position, you may engage in concurrent employment in a cap-subject position as long as you continue to be employed in the cap-exempt position. You may begin working for the cap-subject employer as soon as the cap-subject employer properly files a non-frivolous Form I-129 or as of the requested start date, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As long as you continue cap-exempt employment, were previously counted toward the cap, or otherwise remain cap-exempt, you will not become subject to the H-1B cap again during the same H-1B validity period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing employment terms with the same employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Form I-129 is used to request new employment or a change of employment with the same employer. If your current H-1B employer properly files a non-frivolous Form I-129 requesting new employment or a change of employment, you are authorized to work according to the terms of the new/changed employment once that petition is filed, or as of the requested start date, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use I-129 to request amendments or changes; retain evidence of filing and follow Form I-129 filing instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS final rule — weighted selection process (FY2027)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Dec. 23, 2025, DHS announced a final rule to amend regulations governing the process by which USCIS selects H-1B registrations for unique beneficiaries, implementing a weighted selection process that will favor allocating H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens while maintaining opportunity for employers at all wage levels. The rule is effective Feb. 27, 2026 and in place for FY 2027 H-1B cap registration season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule changes selection mechanics for registrations; petitioners and registrants should consult USCIS guidance for operational details on how weighting affects selection and registration strategy.
